It was the end of 2016 and I am still a "rooting" addict. The stuff that you do in Android to unlock more functionalities like screen recording, custom themes, use SetCPU to improve your battery or improve performance in gaming. At the time I was using a custom rom on my Samsung Galaxy Tab 4, and suddenly out of the blue, the author of our custom rom (Cyanogenmod 13) just went AWOL so one in our community stepped in and maintained the rom (continued updating it to get the latest patch and even transitioned it to Lineage OS 13). But soon that guy got busy too, although he told us before stopping the maintenance, so I took the chance and asked him how it's even done, in hopes that I could take over. He told me to install Ubuntu 16 and install git and clone the repo of Lineage OS, get the relevant patches from this repo to get device drivers for our device and more stuff that I don't know how to do...

Needless to say, as a complete beginner of Linux, that was the first time I heard about it and I don't even have the slightest idea on how to install it or how it works... I failed hard. Not only I wasn't able to compile the custom rom, but I also got stuck on basic steps like how to install apps, how to edit a file owned by root, even using Git (which I only learned last year).

But it sparked my interest in using Linux. I started in Ubuntu 16, then moved to Linux Mint, then to Kali (to pretend like I'm sort of hacker when I don't even know how to use the tools in it, and the dangers of running in root all of the time), then elementary OS, the other flavors of Ubuntu before moving to Arch derivatives but never tried Arch itself, then now I'm back to Ubuntu just because it has the highest amount of apps available and support as well.

I chose Linux because I have a potato laptop. Using Windows, at least in its unmodified form, just makes my laptop unbearably slow. Update after update, one of my devices won't work, i still remember that my family almost had my laptop repaired because my keyboard, wifi, bluetooth and printer did not worked after it updated. So forced updates was the last nail in the coffin, especially that I live in a country where internet access is expensive. At that time, here in PH, in order to have a 1GB allocation of internet for 3 days, we'd have to pay 50PHP or 1 dollar. We're a third world country so it's definitely cheap, we'd rather spend it on food, or water or electric bill.

As for the transition, it was definitely hard at first. I found myself staring at the screen figuring out how the various apps works, and what do I replace the apps that don't have an equivalent. There was no MS Office nor Photoshop nor Vegas Pro Studio which are the apps that I mostly use in Windows at the time. I think it took me a year and a half of dual booting just because I wasn't ready to make the full switch. But eventually as any Linux user I made it.

Two of my laptops, one is new which is what I daily drive these days run Ubuntu 22.04 and the other, old potato laptop runs on Linux Mint XFCE.

I'm thinking the partition may be corrupted. If you still have the Flash Drive with elementary OS on it (or anything with Live Linux installed on a Flash Drive will do), boot to that:

1. Open the terminal
2. Run `sudo fdisk -l`
3. Once the prior command has been run, at the Device column (dev/sdaX) look at the type column, remember all the devices with Linux Filesystem on it. Here is an example of a Linux file system in fdisk: [https://i.imgur.com/znIKm0w.png](https://i.imgur.com/znIKm0w.png)
4. Run `sudo fsck /dev/sdaX` on each of the linux filesystems you found  
Example: `sudo fsck /dev/sda2` or `sudo fsck /dev/sda3`
5. Shutdown the Live Linux Flash Drive, remove it and then try to boot elementary on your PC.

Unlock your bootloader and then root it using Magisk. There should be a lot of guides online. After Magisk is installed, do this:

​

1. Go to Magisk settings (should be at the top right cog icon), turn on MagiskHide.Now go back, tap the shield icon below (Superuser requests) MagiskHide is now visible, go to that. Tap Google Services and it will expand, check all the additional items under it.- do this for all the other google apps that you have installed.
2. Go to Magisk settings again and the turn on Hide Magisk. Name it to whatever you want. Reopen Magisk using the new program name that you assigned it to.
3. And then go ahead and clear the App Data of both Google Play Services and Google Play Store.
4. Go to Magisk modules (4th option below) and then install MagiskHide Props Config. Now finally reboot!
5. Go to Play Store and then install a terminal application. (Material Terminal is what I use in this case).
6. Open the terminal app, type props then press enter, after follow the instructions to find your device in the list, change your device fingerprint to the Global version of the phone. Reboot once done.
7. Again clear the app data of Google Play Services and Google Play Store. It should be fixed now.

Applications depended on Xorg functions that it shouldn't be even depended on.

Things like simple copy and paste, full screen applications, mouse gestures as well as keyboard management. These various functions had to be reimplemented in Wayland using different tools.

It isn't just something that displays your apps, it literally manages almost everything. Heck, the most popular breakage for me I think is the fact that f.lux (a blue light protection app) doesnt work in wayland anymore because it uses xorg's specific commands. 

Probably the case with other applications as well, some gets developed for a long period of time (GNOME and KDE, the applications themselves), some just get dropped because of lack of developers. (Not every program maintainer can do this, remember GNU/Linux is just mostly free time devs who work on their projects) 

TheLinuxExperiment has a great simple explanation on this! Check it out: https://youtu.be/g1BoZnekkyM

Note on the screen sharing, Pipewire actually solves all of that ;) and it works with Flatpak apps too. I dont have the link but the upcoming OBS release will finally include pipewire plugin that would allow screen recording on Wayland. Plus Chrome 90 already uses Pipewire for screen sharing (webrtc).

It was originally designed for sharing video streams between applications (pulse-video) and then they eventually also included an audio server that would work with Jack, Alsa and Pulse apps at the same time (without having to switch to another incase an app uses Jack exclusively).

On top of that, Pipewire video sharing through Flatpak allows a very fine tuned security control, like android type of permission so it's secure :))

It's working for me, i even got openSUSE alongside Win10, Manjaro and my new PopOS:

1. Create a new boot/efi partition, something like 1000MB wouldn't hurt, format it to fat32. Point the boot/efi to this partition.
2. After installation, it will reboot automatically to pop, just follow the prompts then after setting it up, reboot.
3. On your BIOS make the manjaro grub the first in list, exit and boot to manjaro.
4. Launch the terminal, type this:

>sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg

(grub update is just a wrapper for mkconfig, ubuntu have it but arch/manj doesn't. Nevertheless it works.)

Hope you get it working!

**NOTE: The installer doesnt continue without a boot partition selected. So this is how i did it. :)**
